name: Khalidiya Khanqah Mosque and Tekke
description: A Naqshbandi Sufi complex of mosque, tekke, library and market beside Erbil Citadel. It was founded in 1805 by Mullah Hidayatullah al-Arbili at the request of Mawlana Khalid al-Naqshbandi and rebuilt in 1961. The surrounding Khanqah quarter takes its name from it.

name: Melqi (Mar Qardagh tradition), Ankawa
description: Ankawa has been linked to the Neo-Assyrian town of Milqia, seat of an Akitu house of Ishtar near Arbela. Melqi is the martyrdom and burial place of Saint Mar Qardagh in the Syriac History of Mar Qardagh, and the saint is still venerated in Ankawa.
review_notes: Scholarly identification (Parpola) and hagiographic tradition, not an excavated site.

name: Qasr Shemamok (Kilizu)
description: A 20-hectare tell rising about 30 m above the plain, 30 km south of Erbil on the Shiwazor river, with a lower town of about 50 hectares. Under the Assyrians it was Kilizu, a provincial capital; remains run from Hurrian and Assyrian to Parthian and Sasanian times. A French mission has excavated there since 2011.

description: A tell about 30 km south of Erbil, first identified by the Erbil Plain Archaeological Survey in 2012. name: Dwin Castle
description: A castle in the mountain village of Dwin, about 31 km north-east of Erbil, long linked by local tradition to the family of Saladin. Research began in 2014 with Pázmány Péter Catholic University and Salahaddin University; restoration plans were reviewed in 2025.

name: Rabban Boya Shrine
description: A cave shrine at about 1,070 m above Shaqlawa, sacred since early Christian times and shared by Christians and Muslims, who know it as Sheikh Wso Rahman. It was recognised as a historic site in 1945; an old church and cemetery lie nearby.

sources.sourceName: Kurdistan Chronicle — Raban Boya: One Shrine, Two Faiths
Kurdistan Regional Government, Board of Investment — Doing Business in the Kurdistan Region

name: Batas-Harir Rock Relief
description: A rock relief of a standing figure carved on the cliff of Mount Harir above the villages of Batas and Harir. Its date is debated: the dress suggests the Parthian period, and one reading identifies the figure as a ruler of Adiabene of the 1st century AD.

sources.sourceName: World History Encyclopedia — Rock relief of Mountain Hareer

review_notes: Pin is on Harir town (Wikidata), not the relief itself. See Grabowski 2011 for the scholarly study.

name: Dere Castle
description: A ruined castle about 40 km north of Erbil on the Erbil–Rawanduz road. Sources disagree on its age: some attribute it to Muhammad Pasha of Soran in the 19th century, others to an older foundation that was rebuilt.

sources.sourceName: Annali di Ca' Foscari. Serie orientale 60 (2024)

name: Rawanduz Old Town
description: The old quarters of Rawanduz keep narrow lanes and flat-roofed stone houses. Rawanduz was founded by the Rawadid dynasty in the 10th century and was capital of the Soran Emirate until 1836. In 2023 the government began buying and restoring historic houses, starting with ten.

sources.sourceName: Rudaw, 2023 — Government initiates process to preserve Rawanduz historic houses

name: Qalat Lokhan
description: A fortification on the northern edge of Rawanduz, discussed with the other late-Islamic castles of the Soran region.

sources.sourceName: Annali di Ca' Foscari. Serie orientale 60 (2024)

name: Gird-i Dasht
description: The largest known mound in the Soran area, rising about 20 m above the plain. The Rowanduz Archaeological Program excavated and surveyed it from 2013.

sources.sourceName: Academia.edu — Rowanduz Archaeological Program first report
Penn Museum, Expedition 56(3) — Searching for the Kingdom of Musasir

name: Gund-i Topzawa
description: A burned early Iron Age settlement near Sidakan, cut into a hillside and uncovered when road widening in 2013 disturbed it. Radiocarbon dates place its construction in the early 1st millennium BC, and its destruction fits Sargon II’s campaign against Musasir in 714 BC.

sources.sourceName: Penn Museum, Expedition 56(3) — Searching for the Kingdom of Musasir

name: Topzawa Stele
description: A bilingual Urartian–Assyrian stele near Sidakan recording a campaign to Musasir by the Urartian king Rusa I. Sources disagree whether it is still in place or held in Erbil.
review_notes: Current custody disputed (in situ vs. Erbil museum). Year is the approximate reign of Rusa I.

name: Kelashin Stele
description: A stele at the Kelashin pass bearing an Urartian–Akkadian bilingual text of about 800 BC, first described in 1827. It records the Urartian king Ishpuini taking the city of Musasir (Ardini).
review_notes: The stele sits on the Iraq–Iran border; sources disagree on its present custody.

name: Mudjesir (proposed Musasir temple of Haldi)
description: Column bases and statues found in the village of Mudjesir have been linked to the temple of Haldi at Musasir (Ardini), sacked by Sargon II in 714 BC. The identification is a working hypothesis; other candidates lie in Iran.

sources.sourceName: Rudaw, 22 July 2014 — A stunning find in Kurdistan
Penn Museum, Expedition 56(3) — Searching for the Kingdom of Musasir

review_notes: Identification with Musasir is debated.

name: Bestoon Cave
description: A cave in the Bradost mountains south-west of Soran where 1950s work with Fuad Safar found Neolithic remains. It has been developed for visitors.

sources.sourceName: Kurdistan Regional Government, Board of Investment — Doing Business in the Kurdistan Region

name: Diyan Cave
description: A cave on Bradost mountain near Hawdiyan, listed with Bestoon Cave among the heritage destinations of Erbil Governorate.

sources.sourceName: Kurdistan Regional Government, Board of Investment — Doing Business in the Kurdistan Region

review_notes: No archaeological source found yet.

name: Zawi Chemi Shanidar
description: An open-air settlement below Shanidar Cave excavated by Ralph Solecki, important for the transition to settled life in the Zagros.

sources.sourceName: PLOS ONE — The Zagros Epipalaeolithic revisited (Palegawra)

name: Plngan Cave
description: A cave at the foot of Plngan Mountain in Soran where the Soran antiquities department and the Autonomous University of Barcelona reported human footprints and remains of the late Old and early Middle Stone Age in 2025.

sources.sourceName: Rudaw, 17 May 2025 — Stone Age footprints discovered in Soran

name: Bana Helk
description: A hilltop Neolithic village north of Erbil where Kurdish and Spanish archaeologists found Halaf-period remains and decorated pottery.

sources.sourceName: Rudaw, 29 May 2022 — Traces of Halaf culture discovered in north Erbil

name: Mar Gewargis Church, Bedyal
description: The historic church of Bedyal, one of the oldest Christian villages of the Barzan area. In 2025 the Assyrian Church of the East patriarch called for careful restoration of the region’s historic churches.

sources.sourceName: Kurdistan Chronicle — A Christian village in the heart of Kurdistan’s mountains
SyriacPress, 12 August 2025 — Patriarch Mar Awa III on historic churches

name: Old Town of Koya
description: The late-Ottoman old town of Koya (Koy Sanjaq), with architecture rarely found elsewhere in the Kurdistan Region. ALIPH and WADI have funded emergency stabilisation and documentation. The Bayz Agha and Hawawan quarters are among its oldest.

sources.sourceName: ALIPH Foundation — Safeguarding the Old Town of Koya
WADI — Safeguarding the Old Town of Koya

name: Grand Mosque of Koya
description: One of Koya’s oldest landmarks, founded in 1844, with a domed ceiling carrying Qur’anic inscriptions, marble columns and a stone minbar. An archaeological field study was published by Zeidan Rashid in 2013.

sources.sourceName: Annals of the Faculty of Arts, Ain Shams University — Zeidan Rashid, The Great Mosque of Koysinjaq

name: Haji Bakr Agha Qaysari, Koya
description: A covered market of more than 90 shops built in 1840, described as one of the oldest bazaars in Iraqi Kurdistan and still in use.

sources.sourceName: World Monuments Fund on Google Arts & Culture — Qaisari Bazaar in Koya

name: Mahmud Agha Khan, Koya
description: A two-storey stone, gypsum and timber caravanserai of 1861–62 with 64 rooms at the centre of Koya’s bazaar, one of the town’s four old khans. WADI stabilised its endangered structures; Kurdistan24 described it as neglected in 2025.

sources.sourceName: WADI — Safeguarding the Old Town of Koya

name: Mulla Abdul Majid House, Koya
description: A two-storey mud, lime and timber house with two courtyards and a hexagonal fountain, restored as a heritage museum of life about 250 years ago.

name: Mulla Kura House, Koya
description: Described as one of the most prominent historic houses of Koya.

name: Mar Bena Church, Armota
description: A church at Armota near Koya linked to the Monastery of Mar Behnam, said to date from the 4th century. It was destroyed in 1988 and rebuilt in 1996.

sources.sourceName: Mesopotamia Heritage — The Mar Bena church in Koy Sanjaq

name: Mart Mariam Church, Armota
description: The village church of Armota, built in 1868 and renovated in 1979 and 2009. The village also has a church of Mar Michael and a shrine of Mart Shmune.

name: Maltai Rock Reliefs (Halamata Cave)
description: Four Neo-Assyrian reliefs on Mount Zawa, about 7 km south-west of Duhok above Geverke village. Each shows a procession of nine figures: the Assyrian king, most likely Sennacherib (704–681 BC), before gods standing on animals. They belong to his northern canal system. Gertrude Bell photographed them in 1909; they were vandalised in 2016 and again in 2023.

description: A group of Yazidi shrines around the town of Sharya, 15 km south of Duhok. They include Şêx Enzerût, Pîr Afat, Evdê Reş, Nasirdîn, Siltan Êzîd, Şêx Şems, Şahsiwar, Şêxûbekir, Kerecal, Şêx Hesen and Pîr Bûb.
review_notes: Shrine list differs between Wikipedia revisions; individual shrines need separate verification.

name: Khanke Hellenistic Tombs
description: About 40 tombs exposed on the shore of the Mosul Dam reservoir near Khanke when drought lowered the water. Duhok’s antiquities director Bekas Brifkani dates them to the Hellenistic or Seleucid period.

sources.sourceName: CBS News, 30 August 2025 — Ancient tombs discovered in Iraq due to drought

approximateLocation: Mosul Dam reservoir shore, Khanke sub-district

name: Kemune Mittani Palace
description: A Bronze Age palace of the Mittani period on the east bank of the Tigris, exposed by the falling Mosul Dam reservoir in 2018. A German–Kurdish team found walls up to 2 m thick, rare red and blue wall paintings and ten cuneiform tablets; one tablet suggests the city was ancient Zakhiku.

sources.sourceName: University of Tübingen press release — Palace of the Mittani Empire in the Duhok province

approximateLocation: East bank of the Tigris, Mosul Dam reservoir
review_notes: Underwater for most of the year; Zakhiku identification is tentative.

name: Tell Gombass
description: A mound on the Mosul Dam reservoir where Duhok archaeologists reported five superimposed settlement layers, part of a survey of 86 sites made between 2023 and 2025.

sources.sourceName: Shafaq News — Duhok excavations reveal five ancient settlement layers (mirror)
sources.sourceTypeNote: Mirror of a Shafaq News report.

review_notes: Seen only in a search snippet of a mirrored article.

name: Mardaman (Bassetki)
description: A northern Mesopotamian city occupied from about 2900 to 600 BC beside Bassetki village. 92 cuneiform tablets excavated by the University of Tübingen in 2017 identified it as Mardaman, a royal city known from Akkadian and Old Babylonian texts.

sources.sourceName: Heidelberg University — Edition der Texte von Bassetki/Mardama

name: Muqable I
description: A numbered mound in the Bassetki settlement cluster investigated by the University of Tübingen.

name: Muqable III
description: A numbered mound in the Bassetki settlement cluster investigated by the University of Tübingen.

name: Nemrik 9
description: An early Neolithic (Pre-Pottery Neolithic A) settlement of about 1.8 hectares on a Tigris terrace, dated c. 9800–8270 BC. Polish archaeologists excavated its round houses, graves and stone tools in 1985–89 before the Mosul Dam flooded the area.

name: Monastery of Mar Daniel, Bakhetme
description: Local tradition places the martyrdom of Saint Daniel the Physician at Bakhetme and dates his monastery to the 3rd century AD. The village keeps a church of Mar Gewargis; the churches of Mar Daniel and Mart Maryam are recorded as former.
review_notes: Founding date is local tradition.

name: Sourp Vartan Armenian Church, Avzrog
description: An Armenian Apostolic church in Avzrog Miri, a village founded in 1933 by Armenian survivors from near Van; neighbouring Avzrog Shano has an Assyrian church of Mar Gewargis.

name: Kanisban
description: A Neolithic settlement of the 7th millennium BC in the Navkur plain near Rovia, announced in January 2025 by the Duhok antiquities directorate and the University of Udine.

sources.sourceName: Shafaq News, 9 January 2025 — 8,000-year-old Neolithic site discovered in Duhok

name: Asinkran
description: A Navkur-plain site near Rovia with evidence of pottery production and grain processing over 8,000 years old and two buildings of about 7,000 years ago, excavated by Duhok and the University of Udine.

sources.sourceName: Shafaq News, 9 January 2025 — 8,000-year-old Neolithic site discovered in Duhok

name: Zakho Castle
description: The castle in central Zakho on the bank of the Khabur, of which only a tower remains. It is said to have served as the governor’s house under the Bahdinan emirate; its true history is not known.

name: Qubad Pasha Castle
description: A hexagonal structure with six windows and an entrance gate standing in Zakho’s cemetery.

sources.sourceName: Kurdistan24 — Zakho, a Kurdish city with invisible wonders

name: Old Bazaar of Zakho
description: The old market of Zakho, the subject of a 2019 revitalisation and conservation study. A University of Mosul thesis found Zakho’s heritage buildings neglected.

sources.sourceName: Kurdistan24 — Zakho, a Kurdish city with invisible wonders

description: A synagogue in Alqosh with the tomb of the prophet Nahum, the tomb of his sister Sara in the courtyard, a school and a storeroom. The fragile building has been under restoration.

name: St Mary al-Tahira Church, Qaraqosh
description: The most iconic building of Baghdede, with an “ancient” church supposed to be of the 13th century and the great new al-Tahira of the early 20th century. Islamic State used it as a firing range in 2014–16.

name: Mar Yacoub al-Muqataa Church, Qaraqosh
description: Attested in 1712, destroyed by Nader Shah in 1743 and rebuilt in 1744 by the governor of Mosul; the first church of Baghdede assigned to the Catholics.

sources.sourceName: Mesopotamia Heritage — Saint James the Mutilated Church

name: Mart Shmoni Church, Qaraqosh
description: A Syriac Orthodox church whose royal-gate lintel carries 12th-century reliefs of Mart Shmoni’s sons, the Maccabees, with Mongol-style faces and dress.

sources.sourceName: Mesopotamia Heritage — Mart Shmoni Church in Baghdede (Qaraqosh)

name: Mar Sarkis and Bakus Church, Qaraqosh
description: Possibly the first church of Baghdede, confirmed in a late 16th-century manuscript and known for 15th–16th-century ceramic tiles. Islamic State sacked and burned it.

sources.sourceName: Mesopotamia Heritage — Mar Sarkis and Bakus Church in Baghdede

name: Mar Gorgis Church, Qaraqosh
description: A Syriac Orthodox church mentioned in a prayer book of 1270, made of a small rock-cut ancient church and a massive modern one.

sources.sourceName: Mesopotamia Heritage — Mar Gorgis Church in Baghdede (Qaraqosh)

name: Mar Addai Church, Karamles
description: A church of the early 1960s, probably on an older site, where relics attributed to Mar Addai were found in 1881. Its martyrion holds the tomb of Fr Ragheed Ganni, killed in 2007.

sources.sourceName: Mesopotamia Heritage — The Mar Addai church in Karemles

name: Mar Gorgis Church, Bartella
description: A Syriac Catholic church: the ancient building was renovated in the mid-19th century and a new church built in 1934. Islamic State burned it; major repairs followed.

sources.sourceName: Mesopotamia Heritage — The Mar Gorgis church in Bartella

name: Mart Mariam Church, Bartella
description: A Syriac Orthodox church built by the townspeople in the late 19th century from the stones of two churches ruined after the Mongol invasion.

sources.sourceName: Mesopotamia Heritage — Mart Mariam Church in Bartella

name: Mart Shmoni Church, Bartella
description: A Syriac Orthodox church, also called Bney Shmoni after the saint’s seven sons, profaned and partly burned in 2014–16.

sources.sourceName: Mesopotamia Heritage — Mart Shmouni Church in Bartella

description: A three-nave Syriac Orthodox basilica rebuilt in 1890 with marble royal doors.

sources.sourceName: Mesopotamia Heritage — Mart Shmoni church in Baashiqa

description: A Syriac Catholic church built in 1924–32 to replace a church of 1856; profaned during the 2014–16 occupation.

sources.sourceName: Mesopotamia Heritage — Mart Mariam al Adra Church in Baashiqa

description: One of the oldest churches of Alqosh, said to hold the relics of Mar Mikha, a disciple of Mar Awgin.

sources.sourceName: Mesopotamia Heritage — The Church of Mar Mikha in Alqosh

name: Mar Gorgis Church, Alqosh
description: Considered the oldest church of Alqosh; restored in 1681 and rebuilt in 1906. Now a Chaldean cathedral.

sources.sourceName: Mesopotamia Heritage — Mar Gorgis Church in Alqosh

alternativeNames: Chaldean Cathedral of Saint George, Alqosh

sources.sourceName: Mesopotamia Heritage — The Mar Gorgis Church in Baqofa

description: The main church of Tell Esqof, attested in a lectionary of 1499; the old building seen in 1943 was already gone by 1955.

sources.sourceName: Mesopotamia Heritage — The Mar Gorgis Church in Tell Esqof

name: Mar Qouryakos Church, Batnaya
description: Probably the oldest church of Batnaya, destroyed and rebuilt in 1944; the town was left in ruins by the fighting of 2014–16.

sources.sourceName: Mesopotamia Heritage — The Mar Qouryakos Church in Batnaya

name: Yazidi Mausoleums of Bozan
description: Bozan, “Little Lalish”, has many mausoleums, oratories and sacred stones, mostly in its hill cemetery, which serves twelve villages; 70 caves show very early occupation. Several mausoleums date from the 12th century.

sources.sourceName: Mesopotamia Heritage — The Yazidi mausoleums in Bozan

name: Yazidi Mausoleum of Baba Noah, Hatara
description: A Yazidi mausoleum in the village of Hatara near Alqosh, whose tell attests Assyrian-period occupation. Not to be confused with ancient Hatra.

sources.sourceName: Mesopotamia Heritage — The Yazidi Mausoleum of Baba Noah in Hatra

name: Mausoleum of Sheikh Bakeur al-Qatani, Bahzani
description: A rebuilt mausoleum in Bahzani, the intellectual heart of Yazidism with neighbouring Bashiqa; Islamic State destroyed 22 mausoleums in the two towns in 2014–16.

description: A Yazidi mausoleum in Bashiqa destroyed by Islamic State and restored and reopened in January 2018.

name: Mausoleum of Sheikh Suwar, Beban
description: The only Yazidi building with geometric patterns inside its dome and drum, dated by style to the 14th century; destroyed in 1893 and rebuilt.

sources.sourceName: Mesopotamia Heritage — Yazidi mausoleum Sheikh Suwar in Beban

description: The fortress above the Tigris at Tikrit, a town that began as an Assyrian fort and was the birthplace of Saladin, with remains of its old city wall.

name: Al-Arba‘een Mosque, Tikrit
description: An 11th-century five-domed mosque with the shrines of Amr ibn Jundab al-Ghifari and Sitt Nafisa, named for forty martyrs said to lie beneath it and used as an Islamic college in 1262. Islamic State destroyed it on 24 September 2014.
